implementation_notes: Rust keeps the two halves explicit and typed: the recipient set is a Vec computed per message, sequential delivery is a plain for loop over it, and concurrent delivery is futures::future::join_all over a mapped iterator of send futures - FuturesUnordered when results may be consumed out of order or the set is large. Ownership is the real win: each future takes its own clone of the message (or an Arc), so sharing mutable state across recipients is a compile error rather than a review comment. tokio::join! covers only fixed arity, so the dynamic list is always a Vec plus join_all/unordered unless a broker client crate is used.
pitfalls: join_all drives every future on the current task: a blocking send inside deliver blocks the executor thread, so blocking clients belong in spawn_blocking.
join_all re-polls all futures and collects results in order; a very large or streaming recipient set should use FuturesUnordered to avoid the overhead.
Even a failed delivery yields a Result rather than aborting, so `?` on the first element silently discards the remaining outcomes - handle the Vec explicitly.
